name: Tomás Ribeiro (synthetic)

facts.label: computer programming
facts.story: Writes Python jobs that load sensor readings from the electricity grid into PostgreSQL every night.

facts.label: debug software
facts.story: Traces missing-reading problems back through the loader and fixes the cause instead of patching the report.

facts.label: SQL
facts.story: Writes SQL checks that flag gaps in the readings before the morning report goes out.

facts.label: web services
facts.story: Built a small REST service that gives the operations team access to the cleaned readings.

facts.label: tools for software configuration management
facts.story: Keeps every change in Git and runs tests in a CI pipeline before it goes live.

answers.recent_work: For the last three years I've been a developer at a company that runs electricity metering. Mostly Python and PostgreSQL: I maintain the nightly jobs that pull sensor readings in and load them into the database, and I look after the checks on top of that. I'm 38, and we moved here from Porto in Portugal when my husband got a job at a research institute, so this is my first job in Finland.
answers.example: Last winter the morning report kept showing holes for some meters. I went through the loader logs and found that one supplier's files arrived twice with different timestamps, and my job was dropping the second batch. I changed the load to compare the batches properly, and I added a check that raises an alert when a meter has no readings for six hours. After that the holes were gone.
answers.tools: Python every day, with pandas for the cleaning, and PostgreSQL for storage. SQL for the checks. Git and a CI pipeline, so every change gets tested before it goes live. I read logs a lot, honestly. Cloud-wise I only know the basics, we run on a few virtual machines.
answers.people: I work in a team of five. The operations team are the ones who read my data every morning, so I meet them weekly and show what changed. Their questions usually decide what I fix next. The data owner at the supplier I only deal with by email, mostly when files are late.
answers.beyond: Before this I studied physics and did my master's thesis on sensor calibration, so I'm comfortable with measurement data. I also volunteer as a mentor on a beginners' coding course on Saturdays, where I help people with their first Python scripts.
answers.open_floor: Only that I like work where the data actually matters to someone, so I check what the people downstream need instead of just delivering a table.
answers.looking_for: Data engineering, or backend work close to data. English at work, I'm learning Finnish but I can't work in it yet. Hybrid would be best, and I could start within a month or two.

probes: On a typical night the job pulls around forty files from the supplier's server, validates the columns, and loads them in one transaction. I wrote the validation myself: it checks that the timestamps are in order, that the units are the expected ones, and that no meter appears twice in the same file.

One example of the SQL checks: I wrote a query that lists every meter with fewer readings than its neighbours in the same area, and the operations team used it each morning to decide which sites to call about.
